sources.title: Tarsila do Amaral (Q466627), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-02): label 'Tarsila do Amaral', description 'Brazilian painter (1886-1973)', born 1 September 1886, died 17 January 1973, citizenship Brazil, Korean label present. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

'Tarsila do Amaral', Encyclopaedia Britannica, read in full. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: presents her as a Brazilian painter who blended local Brazilian content with international avant-garde aesthetics; gives her training (academic painting from 1916, Academie Julian from 1920, Lhote, briefly Leger and Gleizes from December 1922), A Negra (1923) as the start of her synthesis, the 1923-24 trips with Oswald de Andrade and Blaise Cendrars that opened the Pau-Brasil phase, Abaporu (1928) as the painting that inspired Andrade's Anthropophagite Manifesto, and the later social and neo-Pau-Brasil phases. Encyclopedic overview; admiring in tone, little critical voice.

'Tarsila do Amaral: Inventing Modern Art in Brazil' (11 February - 3 June 2018), exhibition page, Museum of Modern Art, New York, read: sets out her studies (piano, sculpture and drawing, then the Academie Julian in Paris from 1920, then Lhote, Gleizes and Leger, her 'military service in Cubism'), her quoted aim 'I want to be the painter of my country', Abaporu as the painting that inspired the Manifesto of Anthropophagy, and states that this is the first exhibition in the United States devoted exclusively to her. Curated institutional text; promotional.

'Tarsila do Amaral', Enciclopedia Itau Cultural (Portuguese), read in full: dated chronology of her teachers (the sculptor William Zadig 1916, Pedro Alexandrino 1917, Georg Elpons, Emile Renard and the Academie Julian in Paris 1920, Albert Gleizes 1923), the founding of the Grupo dos Cinco after the 1922 Semana de Arte Moderna, the move from cubist-inspired work to Brazilian figuration (A Negra, A Caipirinha 1923), Pau-Brasil (1924), Abaporu (1928) and the anthropophagic movement, the 1933 social pictures, the neo Pau-Brasil phase of the late 1940s, the first retrospective at the Museu de Arte Moderna de Sao Paulo in 1950, two murals in 1954 and 1956, and the 2019 MASP exhibition 'Tarsila Popular' (record 400,000 visitors in three months). Institutional encyclopedia with footnoted bibliography; admiring in tone.

Review of 'Tarsila do Amaral: Inventing Modern Art in Brazil', Studio International (2018), read in full: an enthusiastic review that says the exhibition shows her to have 'invented' Brazilian modernism, recounts her Paris study with Gleizes and Lhote and her internship with Leger (the 'sub-Legers' who performed 'military service' in cubism), quotes her 'I want to be the painter of my country', describes Abaporu as devised to startle Oswald de Andrade and as the seed of the manifestos, notes the Paris frames and the later 'drier and more brittle' social paintings, and calls the anthropophagy theory 'something of a turnoff' to read. Independent press reviewer; admiring of the 1920s work, critical of the manifesto and of the exhibition's cut-off.

Elisa Wouk Almino, 'How Tarsila do Amaral Reinvented Brazilian Identity with Modern Art', Hyperallergic (2018), read in full: a Brazilian critic's account of the MoMA exhibition; says Brazilian textbooks treat her as the first artist to develop distinctly Brazilian art in the twentieth century, reports her letter that after two months in Paris she felt 'increasingly Brazilian' and wanted to be 'the painter of my country', reports the curator's view that her pastel palette was a deliberate and 'confrontational' choice, says she exhibited A Negra only twice in her lifetime and that the museum under-addresses race and privilege, and notes the later reception through the 1960s artists and Tropicalia. Independent, partly critical press.

Vitoria Hadba Groom, review of 'Tarsila do Amaral: Inventing Modern Art in Brazil', The Brooklyn Rail (March 2018), read in full: a Brazilian art historian says the show presents a beautiful but one-dimensional view of a complex artist, 'para gringo ver', says the artist 'had reservations regarding Cubism' while Leger's influence 'is undeniable', notes she realised the racism embedded in A Negra and avoided exhibiting it, records that her 1930s work became more socially engaged, and that the Paris show frames were commissioned from Pierre Legrain. Independent, critical press.

Luis Perez-Oramas, 'Tarsila, Melancholic Cannibal' (part 2), essay from the exhibition catalogue, published on post.moma.org, read in full: a curator's scholarly essay that argues her work is not simply Cubist (quoting Herkenhoff that she 'never fully understood' Cubist logic, a point that 'does not detract' from her founding role), reads her limited repertoire of repeated forms as an ornamental geometry close to Art Deco, reports that for her first Paris solo show (Galerie Percier, 1926) she commissioned a different frame from the designer Pierre Legrain for each painting, repeated for the second show, and records Aracy Amaral's contrary reading of the frames as 'a sign of insecurity'; also records that her contact with modern art before 1922 was limited and that she came to modernity 'late'. Curator essay from the organising museum; contested and partly critical.

'Working Men and Women' exhibition text on Tarsila do Amaral, Guggenheim Museum Bilbao, read (short passage): says that after separating from Oswald de Andrade she was 'deeply affected' by the New York stock exchange crash of late 1929, that her properties were mortgaged and she had to adapt to a much more modest lifestyle, and that she continued to look at work and at women in the workforce. Short institutional text; used only for the dated material fact of the 1929 losses, not scored.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_tarsila_britannica, src_tarsila_itau, src_tarsila_studiointl, src_tarsila_hyperallergic, src_tarsila_momapost | 1923-1930 | encyclopedia, institutional encyclopedia, two press reviews, curator essay] Britannica and the Itau encyclopedia agree that from A Negra (1923) she fused Cubist-derived planes with Brazilian subjects and palette into a style of her own; Hyperallergic records her replacing the European nude bather with a Brazilian black woman and painting favela hills and Amazonian flowers as serious subjects, and Studio International calls her rethinking of modernism a 'reverse palimpsest'. The counter-voices (Herkenhoff and Perez-Oramas: not really Cubist, closer to Art Deco ornament) argue about what her style was derived from, not that it was an individual solution, so the row stays at a clear but not extreme level; most sources are exhibition-driven and admiring.

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_tarsila_momapost, src_tarsila_hyperallergic, src_tarsila_itau | 1924-1928 | curator essay, press, institutional encyclopedia] Her own phrase for the palette she favoured, 'ugly' colours (a pure blue, violet pink, vivid yellow, singing green), is recorded in the Itau encyclopedia, and a curator quoted by Hyperallergic calls the pastel choices deliberate and 'confrontational'; for her 1926 and 1928 Paris shows she commissioned a separate frame from the designer Pierre Legrain for each painting, which Perez-Oramas reads as an authorial decision while Aracy Amaral reads it as insecurity. The two readings disagree on motive, so only the documented attention to colour and presentation is scored. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 72 / 0.56 because the strongest items are a curator's interpretation and a contested reading of the frames, with no independent contemporaneous account.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_tarsila_itau, src_tarsila_moma, src_tarsila_studiointl, src_tarsila_momapost | 1916-1923 | institutional encyclopedia, exhibition page, press, curator essay] She moved through a sequence of teachers (a sculptor in 1916, Alexandrino, Elpons, Renard and the Academie Julian, then Lhote, Gleizes and Leger), left the conventional academic course in 1923 to study modern technique, and described her Cubist apprenticeship as 'military service'; Studio International says she 'cherry-picked' their teaching. The curator essay says she never fully mastered Cubist logic and came to modern art late, so the row records sustained deliberate study, not mastery of a specific idiom.

adaptability.rationale: [src_tarsila_itau, src_tarsila_britannica, src_tarsila_guggenheim | 1923-1956 | institutional encyclopedia, encyclopedia, institutional text] Both reference sources document successive changes in her painting: Cubist-inspired Paris studies, the geometric Pau-Brasil pictures, the organic and dreamlike anthropophagic pictures of 1928-29, the more realist pictures after 1933, a modelled neo Pau-Brasil style from the later 1940s, and two commissioned murals in 1954 and 1956; the Guggenheim text notes she had to adjust to a much more modest way of life after the 1929 crash. The causes of the changes in the 1930s are not scored here, and the sources are admiring surveys rather than behavioural accounts.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_tarsila_itau, src_tarsila_hyperallergic, src_tarsila_momapost, src_tarsila_rail | 1920-1928 | institutional encyclopedia, press, curator essay] After the 1922 Semana she went to the conventional route of Paris study but turned her subjects to Brazilian themes in a conservative, Eurocentric art world, which Hyperallergic frames as a deliberate break; the Itau encyclopedia says she distanced herself from conventional academic education to study modern techniques, and the Rail critic says she had reservations about Cubism even while accepting its influence. These are third-party summaries of her choices; the strongest statements about her intent rest on her own letters as quoted by critics.

collaboration.rationale: [src_tarsila_itau, src_tarsila_britannica, src_tarsila_studiointl | 1922-1929 | institutional encyclopedia, encyclopedia, press] She is documented as a founding member of the Grupo dos Cinco with Anita Malfatti, Mario and Oswald de Andrade and Menotti del Picchia, travelled in 1924 with Oswald de Andrade and Blaise Cendrars to Rio at Carnival and to the baroque mining towns, painted the portraits of Mario and Oswald, and illustrated the manifestos and poetry written by Oswald (Studio International); Abaporu and the anthropophagy movement were a two-way exchange with a writer. All sources describe the group at the level of a summary, so the row reflects sustained work inside a circle, not a specific working method.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_tarsila_moma, src_tarsila_studiointl, src_tarsila_hyperallergic, src_tarsila_rail | 1920s | exhibition page, two press reviews, critical review] Her stated aim 'I want to be the painter of my country' is quoted by MoMA, Studio International, Hyperallergic and the Rail (the dating differs between MoMA, which gives 1923, and Hyperallergic, which places it two months into her first Paris stay); the Rail critic says she was 'actively and consciously' trying to create a Brazilian aesthetic. The evidence is her own statement relayed by exhibition-driven writers, and the Rail and Hyperallergic reviewers also argue that her 'Brazilianness' was shaped by privilege, so the row is held low.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_tarsila_itau, src_tarsila_britannica, src_tarsila_momapost | 1920-1928 | institutional encyclopedia, encyclopedia, curator essay] She went to Paris in 1920 'to make contact with European production and perfect herself' (Itau), went back in December 1922 and again in 1923 to study modern technique, set out with friends in 1924 on trips to rediscover Brazilian places that she then painted, and staged solo shows at the Galerie Percier in Paris in 1926 and again two years later with commissioned frames and a catalogue essay by Blaise Cendrars. The evidence is a documented sequence of self-started steps in her career, but it does not show how much was organised by her and how much by her circle.

portrait.reason: No rights-clear portrait found. The only Wikidata P18 image ('Tarsila do Amaral, ca. 1925.jpg', from the O Estado de S. Paulo periodicals section of the Biblioteca Mario de Andrade) has an unknown author and its only basis on the Commons page is a jurisdiction-only tag (public domain for Brazilian media, expired in the US), which is not a documented rights basis; the cropped copy 'Tarsila (cropped).jpg' has the same unnamed-photographer problem. The two Arquivo Nacional Correio da Manha photographs on Commons (accession BR_RJANRIO_PH_0_FOT_08464_0002 and _0005; one dated 19 March 1969) have an unknown photographer and rest on a generic 'government work' tag for a newspaper-company photograph held by a public archive, which does not establish that the photograph itself is out of copyright (a 1969 photograph in Brazil would still have been protected in 1996). The 1929 group photograph with Pagu, Anita Malfatti, Oswald de Andrade and others is a scene taken from a 1975 book. The MoMA mid-1920s profile portrait is in the Pedro Correa do Lago private collection, and her painted self-portraits are held by a licensing estate. Next step: a dated photograph with a named photographer who died before 1955, or an institution page that states reuse terms for a portrait photograph (for example the Instituto Tarsila do Amaral or the Biblioteca Mario de Andrade periodicals collection with item-level terms), or a licence from the estate.
